The recorder is a European woodwind aerophone of the duct-flute family, Hornbostel–Sachs number 421.221.12. It sounds through a thumb hole and seven fingerholes; the bore runs from a reverse cone gradually to a cylinder, and the usual sizes are descant, treble, tenor and bass. The player controls pitch and timbre by opening and closing the holes and by forked fingerings, and it can be played solo or in consort, as well as in historically informed performance, amateur playing and music teaching.
直笛為歐洲氣鳴樂器，最早文獻見於中世紀歐洲；1388年德比伯爵（後為亨利四世）家: The recorder is a European aerophone whose earliest documentation is in medieval Europe; the household accounts of the Earl of Derby (later Henry IV) in 1388 record the name of the recorder, and it enters English literature in the fifteenth century. It was popular in the Renaissance and Baroque periods and little used in the Classical and Romantic; in the twentieth century it was revived by the historically informed performance movement and became an amateur and educational instrument. Monteverdi, Lully, Purcell, Handel, Vivaldi, Telemann, Bach, Hindemith and Berio wrote for it. In 1673 French professionals brought the Baroque recorder to England, where its name was confused with the transverse flute, and from the 1720s it was distinguished by qualifiers such as 'English flute'.

Acoustically the timbre is fairly pure: when the edge sits in the middle of the airstream the odd overtones dominate, and when the edge is clearly off centre the overtones are more evenly spread. The range of the common sizes is given by the lowest note, for example the lowest note of the descant recorder is C5, and the Baroque descant recorder ranges from about C5 to C7. Unlike other instruments of the fipple-flute family, it has a thumb hole above and seven fingerholes. The source does not state how volume is controlled.
